rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Bḍ explains a clear proof as evidence verifying Hūd’s claim to be a prophet sent by God.
rows.anchor: clear evidence that testifies to the truthfulness of his claim to being a prophet sent by God (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Bḍ says Hūd’s people failed to see his clear proofs because they obstinately rejected his message.
rows.anchor: unable to see the clear proofs brought by Hūd because of their obstinacy in rejecting his message (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Kl reads the accusation as claiming Hūd was a madman under an idol’s spell because he cursed it and urged the people to stop idol worship.
rows.anchor: put under a spell by one of their idols, because he had cursed it and had called his people to cease worshipping idols (Kl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Makkan idolaters likewise accused Muhammad of madness or possession, as these cited verses attest.
rows.anchor: The Makkan idolaters, likewise, had accused the Prophet Muhammad of being mad or possessed; see 15:6; 23:70; 34:8; 37:36;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other prophets make similar statements about the beliefs of the people to whom they were sent.
rows.anchor: For similar statements made by prophets concerning the beliefs of the people to whom they had been sent, see also 6:19; 6:78.

rows.speaker: N
rows.claim: N notes that Hūd addresses his challenge to both his people and their gods.
rows.anchor: Hūd’s challenge, which is addressed to his people and their gods (N), to scheme and grant him no respite means

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Kl explains the challenge as meaning that neither the people nor their gods can do anything against Hūd.
rows.anchor: means, “Neither you nor your gods will be able to do anything!” (Kl). Hūd then provides them

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Hūd’s firm reliance on God is the reason he is confident that his opponents cannot scheme against him.
rows.anchor: reason for his confidence in their inability to scheme against him, namely, his firm and unshakeable reliance upon God (Kl)

words: مَا مِن دَآبَّةٍ إِلَّا هُوَ ءَاخِذٌۢ بِنَاصِيَتِهَآ
rows.speaker: N
rows.claim: The forelock image metaphorically expresses that all creatures are under God’s control and authority.
rows.anchor: There is no creature that crawls, but that He holds it by its forelock is a metaphor to denote that all creatures are under God’s Control and Authority (N).

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The straight path means God is on the path of truth, is just, and does not let wrongdoers escape Him.
rows.anchor: Truly my Lord is upon a straight path means that God is upon the path of truth, is Just, and does not let wrongdoers escape Him.

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The straight path also means God will not forsake a person who relies upon Him.
rows.anchor: It also means that He will not forsake one who relies upon Him (Z). Regarding straight path, see 1:6c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment of Thamūd is said to have been an earthquake accompanied by a terrible loud sound, hence its name the Cry.
rows.anchor: punishment that befell the Thamūd is said to have been an earthquake (7:78) accompanied by a terrible, loud sound, which

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited commentary explains why morning found them lifeless as if they had never lived there; the wording recurs in 11:94–95.
rows.anchor: which explains why morning found them lying lifeless in their abode, as though they had never dwelt there (see the identical wording in vv. 94–95; cf. 7:78).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Shuʿayb is also related in the cited passages of the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: For the story of Shuʿayb, see also 7:85–93; 26:176–89.

rows.speaker: Muslim authorities
rows.claim: Many Muslim authorities identify Shuʿayb, an Arabian prophet, with Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses.
rows.anchor: Shuʿayb was also an Arabian prophet who is identified by many Muslim authorities with the Biblical figure Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuʿayb was sent to Midian, whose people lived in northwestern Arabia.
rows.anchor: Shuʿayb was sent to the people of Midian, who resided in northwestern Arabia; see 7:85c.

words: ٱعْبُدُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ مَا لَكُم مِّنْ إِلَٰهٍ غَيْرُهُۥ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like other prophets, Shuʿayb calls his people to worship the one God.
rows.anchor: Like other prophets, he called his people to worship the One God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commands not to diminish measure and balance and to observe them fully with justice call for honesty in business dealings.
rows.anchor: meaning that the Midianites should be honest in their business relations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The full-measure command is also made in the cited passages.
rows.anchor: observe fully the measure and the balance with justice (cf. 7:85; 26:181–82)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not diminishing people’s goods means giving them the full quantity for which they paid.
rows.anchor: that they should give people the full measure of what they paid for—which was also a problem among the Makkan idolaters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Short measure was also a problem among the Makkan idolaters in the Prophet’s time, as Sūrah 83 indicates.
rows.anchor: which was also a problem among the Makkan idolaters during the time of the Prophet; see Sūrah 83.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuʿayb’s warning against corruption on earth is also discussed at 7:85.
rows.anchor: For Shuʿayb’s call to his people to behave not wickedly upon the earth, working corruption, see 7:85c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baqiyyah literally means a remainder or that which remains.
rows.anchor: baqiyyah literally means“remainder” or “that which remains.”

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One reading is that honest wealth given by God is better than fraudulent gain; the remnant is what remains after full measure and avoiding the illicit.
rows.anchor: The wealth that is obtained through honest commercial practices and given by God is better than the gains acquired through fraudulent ones (R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Alternatively, the remnant means God’s reward or Contentment, superior because it abides in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Alternately, it can refer to the reward that is with God or His Contentment, which is greater than what is gained through the act of defrauding (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an repeatedly insists that Muhammad is not a keeper or guardian over his people.
rows.anchor: For the Quranic insistence that the Prophet Muhammad is not a keeper or guardian over his people, see 4:80; 6:66, 104, 107;

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators take the Midianites’ question about Shuʿayb’s prayers as mockery.
rows.anchor: Some commentators note that the Midianites’ question here is a form of mockery (Kl, Q).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q says the sarcastic praise suggests Shuʿayb has forbearance and sound judgment only in his own estimation.
rows.anchor: they intimate that he has these qualities only in his own opinion (Q). The implication is thus that the Midianites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrogant Midianites dismissed Shuʿayb’s message and called him bewitched and a liar.
rows.anchor: The implication is thus that the Midianites, who were arrogant (7:88), did not take seriously Shuʿayb’s message, instead referring to him as

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuʿayb’s clear proof is said to consist of miracles God grants prophets to prove their veracity.
rows.anchor: which are given to all prophets by God to prove their veracity; see 7:85c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The familiar expression says that success and its blessing in this world and the next ultimately depend on God.
rows.anchor: it conveys the idea that no matter what one does, it is ultimately up to God whether it will be successful and carry a blessing in this world and in the next.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuʿayb’s reliance and turning to God echoes the statement taught to the Prophet and links to the earlier Shuʿayb passage.
rows.anchor: Shuʿayb’s statement In Him do I trust and unto Him do I turn is identical to the statement the Prophet is taught to make in 42:10; see also 7:88–89c.

rows.speaker: AF, Kl, My
rows.claim: AF, Kl, and My identify the supplication of truth with the shahādah, “There is no god but God.”
rows.anchor: lā ilāha illa’Llāh; AF, Kl, My

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More broadly, the phrase can mean any supplication that God accepts and answers, as in 40:60.
rows.anchor: More generally, it can refer to any form of supplication that God accepts and to which He responds, as in 40:60: Call upon Me, and I shall respond to you

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Kl explains that true supplication is directed to God, while supplication to anything else is futile.
rows.anchor: The supplication of truth therefore is supplication to God, whereas the supplication to what is other than Him is futile (Kl)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Those whom disbelievers supplicate apart from God are idols and false gods.
rows.anchor: as is the case with those whom they—that is, the disbelievers—supplicate apart from Him, namely, idols and false gods (Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: False gods cannot hear or answer because they have no power to bring harm or benefit; other verses stress their powerlessness.
rows.anchor: The false gods that people call upon other than God answer them not in the least, because they do not have the ability to bring about harm or benefit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Last Day, the false gods will not be able to answer those who called to them for help.
rows.anchor: This is why, on the Last Day, they will not be able to answer those who called upon them for help

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The analogy likens futile invocation to hands stretched toward water that cannot perceive the gesture, just as false gods cannot hear or respond.
rows.anchor: just as the water cannot perceive that his hands are outstretched for it, so too are those whom one calls upon apart from God unable to hear his supplications and respond to them (Z).

words: وَمَا دُعَآءُ ٱلْكَٰفِرِينَ إِلَّا فِى ضَلَٰلٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing statement repeats a portion of 40:50.
rows.anchor: And the supplication of the disbelievers is naught but astray is identical to a portion of 40:50.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prostration motif is also found in the cited passages.
rows.anchor: Cf. 16:48–49; 22:18. Prostrates here expresses the idea of submission, lowliness

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R explains prostration as submission, lowliness, and inability to refuse; 19:93 describes every creature as a servant.
rows.anchor: submission, lowliness, and the inability to refuse (R), which is why 19:93 says, There is none in the heavens and on the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All things are existentially submitted to God at every moment: some recognize this willingly, while others submit unwittingly.
rows.anchor: all things at all moments are “prostrate,” that is, submitted existentially before God: either they understand this state of affairs and prostrate voluntarily in recognition of it, or they prostrate involuntarily and unwittingly

rows.speaker: al-Maybudī
rows.claim: Al-Maybudī says willing prostration submits to God without hope of reward, while unwilling prostration seeks a benefit or escape from harm.
rows.anchor: al-Maybudī says that a prostration is done willingly when one submits to God’s Command and Majesty without any hope of reward or gain; the prostration done unwillingly occurs

rows.speaker: M
rows.claim: M says that shadows also submit to God, showing that every aspect of beings is under His sway.
rows.anchor: As do their shadows is a way of saying that even their shadows submit to God (M), which means that every aspect of their being is under His Sway

rows.speaker: N
rows.claim: N takes morning and evening to imply that creation submits perpetually.
rows.anchor: and in the morning and the evening implies that they do so perpetually (N). See also 16:48

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: The verse offers two similitudes to illustrate truth and falsehood.
rows.anchor: This verse provides two similitudes concerning truth and falsehood (Bg). In the first similitude, the water

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: In the water simile, the torrent churns up impurities that form useless froth and attach to trees and valley sides.
rows.anchor: dirt and impurities, forming a swelling froth, which goes on to become attached to trees and the sides of valleys (Bg) and is basically useless.

words: وَأَمَّا مَا يَنفَعُ ٱلنَّاسَ فَيَمْكُثُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ
rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: Once the torrent subsides, its water becomes pure and useful to people in many ways.
rows.anchor: When the torrent subsides, the water returns to its pure state (Bg) and is then useful to people in numerous ways.

rows.speaker: JJ, Kl
rows.claim: The metal simile describes heating gold, silver, or copper ores to purify them and extract the desired metals; impurities rise as froth.
rows.anchor: when retrieving precious metals such as gold, silver, or copper from the earth (JJ, Kl), the ores are heated over fire in order to purify them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falsehood passes away like froth, while truth, like pure water and precious metals that benefit people, remains; 17:81 makes the same point.
rows.anchor: Falsehood, like the scum generated by the torrent

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Humanity’s creation from a drop of fluid evokes essential weakness and helplessness.
rows.anchor: That human beings were created from a drop of fluid (cf. 18:37; 22:5; 23:12–14; 35:11; 40:67; 53:45–46; 75:37; 76:2; 80:19) evokes their essential weakness (IK)

rows.speaker: IK, Z
rows.claim: People become manifest adversaries of their Lord by denying His power and the blessings He has given them.
rows.anchor: Human beings are a manifest adversary of the Lord (IK, Z) insofar as they deny His Power and the blessings He has bestowed upon them

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Their enmity includes refusing to believe God can resurrect the dead.
rows.anchor: and refuse to believe in His ability to resurrect the dead (R), although they were created to be servants

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Although created to serve God, humans oppose Him.
rows.anchor: although they were created to be servants (51:56), not opponents (IK). This verse was reportedly revealed

rows.speaker: W
rows.claim: The verse was reportedly revealed about Ubayy ibn Khalaf, who doubted that God could resurrect the dead.
rows.anchor: This verse was reportedly revealed in reference to Ubayy ibn Khalaf, a Makkan who expressed skepticism about God’s ability to resurrect the dead (W).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s wording about creation from a drop is echoed in 36:77.
rows.anchor: See also commentary on 36:77: Has not man seen that We created him from a drop and, behold, he is a manifest adversary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nearly identical verse appears at 21:31.
rows.anchor: A nearly identical verse is 21:31; see 21:30–31c. God’s casting or placing firm mountains

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountains stabilize the earth so it does not shake beneath humanity.
rows.anchor: God’s casting or placing firm mountains into the earth for humanity suggests their functioning as a source of stability for the earth, lest it shake beneath them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere mountains are described as stakes that hold up a tent.
rows.anchor: where the mountains are described as stakes like those that hold up a tent.

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī suggests mountains and streams are paired because most streams originate in mountain springs.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī suggests that mountains and streams are mentioned together (cf. 13:3; 27:61), because most streams have their origin in mountain springs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stability of mountains will be overturned on the Last Day, when earth and mountains shake and mountains become shifting sand heaps.
rows.anchor: The stability provided by the mountains will be overturned on the Last Day, however, which is described as a day on which the earth and the mountains shake

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idea that every human community received a messenger also appears in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: Regarding the idea that every community of human beings has been sent a messenger, see also 10:47: For every community there is a messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere the Qur’an says every community will have a witness and will be called to its book.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere in the Quran it is said that for every community there will be a witness (4:41; 16:84; 28:75) and that every community is called to its book (45:28).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship of God is the heart of every revealed message, taught directly by several prophets and summarized at 21:25.
rows.anchor: The command to worship God is understood to be the heart of every revealed message and is uttered directly by several prophets, including Jesus (5:72, 117); Noah

rows.speaker: Ashʿarite theologians
rows.claim: Ashʿarites read the passage to mean that after revelation God guides some to belief and causes others to disbelieve.
rows.anchor: Ashʿarite theologians suggest that among them were those whom God guided; and among them were those who were deserving of error (see also 7:30c) means that, after revealing the message to all, God guides some

rows.speaker: Muʿtazilite commentators
rows.claim: Muʿtazilites take deserving of error to show that misguidance is earned through moral choice, not compelled by God.
rows.anchor: Muʿtazilite commentators, however, adduce the phrase deserving of error

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an elsewhere says God leads wrongdoers astray, including those who mislead others.
rows.anchor: For example, the Quran indicates that God leads astray wrongdoers in particular (14:27; R) or those who have led others astray (see v. 37).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The journey command urges people to learn the fate of earlier deniers; it particularly addresses Arabs who reportedly passed destroyed peoples’ ruins while traveling, but applies more widely.
rows.anchor: The recommendation that one should journey upon the earth in order to learn the fate of earlier disbelieving people refers in particular to the Arabs, who reportedly would pass by the ruins of destroyed peoples

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spiritual value of journeying in general is discussed at 30:9.
rows.anchor: Regarding the spiritual value of journeying in general, see 30:9c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As God brings milk from cattle, honey from bees, and the Hour from the unseen, He also brings humans from their mothers’ wombs.
rows.anchor: Just as God brings things forth from hidden places—milk from the bellies of cattle (v. 66), honey from the bellies of bees (v. 69), and the Hour from the realm of the Unseen (v. 77)—so does He bring forth human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People are born knowing nothing; together with 16:70 and 30:54, this shows that strength and knowledge wax and wane through life.
rows.anchor: Human beings are born knowing naught; see v. 70 and 30:54, which together indicate that human beings’ strength and knowledge wax and wane throughout the course of their lives.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hearing, sight, and hearts are repeatedly grouped as divine gifts.
rows.anchor: Hearing, sight, and hearts are repeatedly mentioned all together or in various combinations as Divine gifts (10:31; 23:78; 32:9).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These faculties enable people to receive guidance and acquire religious knowledge and understanding.
rows.anchor: These are the faculties through which guidance is received and through which religious knowledge and understanding are acquired (22:46)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some people’s faculties become corrupted and impervious to divine guidance.
rows.anchor: but the Quran states that these faculties are corrupted in some human beings, so that they become impervious to Divine Guidance
